nameStory: The 'Korean' part is straightforward - this shrub is native to Korea and Japan. The 'spice' comes from its incredibly fragrant flowers that smell like a warm blend of cloves and vanilla, perfuming entire gardens in spring. Some say the scent is so rich and spicy-sweet, it's like nature's own potpourri!
description: Korean spice viburnum is a compact, bushy deciduous shrub that grows about 7 feet tall and equally wide. It's beloved by gardeners for its spectacular spring flower display and intoxicating fragrance. The shrub has a rounded, dense growth habit with oval leaves that emerge with beautiful copper tones in spring. While native to Asia, it's been planted throughout New England as an ornamental shrub.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Round, dome-shaped clusters of small flowers that start as deep pink-red buds and open to pale pink or white blooms in late spring. The fragrance is unmistakable - intensely spicy-sweet and detectable from several feet away.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stems. Young leaves emerge with a distinctive copper or bronze color before turning green. The leaves feel slightly fuzzy and have a soft texture with visible veining.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small oval berries that start red in late summer, then ripen to glossy black in fall. The fruits are about the size of small peas and often attract birds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, rounded shrub typically 6-7 feet tall and wide at maturity. Branches spread outward creating a full, bushy appearance with multiple stems from the base.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Flower buds are plump and deep reddish-pink, clustered in rounded groups at branch tips. They're quite noticeable in late winter and early spring before opening.

habitat: Korean spice viburnum is primarily found in cultivated settings throughout New England - parks, botanical gardens, residential landscapes, and arboretums. It prefers well-drained soil and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. Since it's not native and has limited naturalization, you're most likely to encounter it in designed landscapes rather than wild areas.

seasonality.spring: The star season - copper-colored new leaves emerge, followed by the spectacular fragrant flower display in late spring. The intense spicy-sweet scent makes this shrub detectable by smell alone during peak bloom.
seasonality.summer: Green foliage provides a quiet backdrop. Small red berries begin forming where flowers were, gradually developing through the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen from red to glossy black, and leaves may show modest yellow fall color before dropping. The berry clusters become more prominent as a identifying feature.
seasonality.winter: Bare branched shrub with distinctive rounded growth form. The plump, reddish flower buds clustered at branch tips are the best winter identification feature.

funFact: Korean spice viburnum was introduced to the Western world thanks to a British diplomat named William Richard Carles, who collected plants while stationed in Korea in the 1880s - that's why the scientific name is 'carlesii'! His botanical collecting was essentially a side hobby to his day job in international relations.
confusionNotes: Other viburnum species can look similar, but Korean spice viburnum's incredibly intense, spicy-sweet fragrance during bloom is unmistakable - no other viburnum in New England smells quite this strong. The copper-colored young leaves are also distinctive among viburnums.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'arrowwood' in some references, Korean spice viburnum isn't the classic 'arrowwood' that most botanists think of - that's typically southern arrowwood (Viburnum dentatum). The name confusion comes from multiple viburnum species being called arrowwood historically.
compareHints: Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size. Native viburnums like hobblebush are much larger and less fragrant, while arrowwoods have more serrated leaves and different flower clusters. The copper-toned young foliage and intensely scented, rounded flower clusters make Korean spice viburnum quite distinctive in the viburnum family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
